114:→ pricing schemes localized to a cordon reliably cut car trips 10–25% within that zone inside one year, while free-transit and cycle-lane schemes show markedly smaller or slower car-specific effects over the same horizon
115:→ multiplying each lever's typical geographic coverage by its per-exposed-commuter effectiveness brackets a citywide 3-year reduction of roughly 1–8.75% for pricing, 0.3–5.6% for free transit, and 0.2–3% for cycle lanes, applied alone
116:→ even the most optimistic single-lever bracket falls well short of a 20% citywide cut within 3 years
128:→ congestion pricing modifies the cost of using existing roads and needs only enforcement-technology rollout, so its measured effects appear within months of legal implementation in every priced case examined
129:→ protected cycle-lane networks and most transit-capacity upgrades require a construction/procurement lead time before any commuter can respond, and the mode-share response itself then unfolds over multiple additional years
130:→ a 3-year policy window allocates a much larger share of its available time to pure waiting for infrastructure-dependent levers than for pricing, shrinking the response time actually available to change behavior
138:→ the two cities that put congestion pricing to a vote before residents had experienced it rejected the scheme by roughly 3-to-1 or 4-to-1 margins
139:→ the one city that let residents experience a time-limited trial before voting saw support rise from a pre-trial minority to a post-trial majority, and the scheme passed
140:→ political feasibility of congestion pricing is strongly sensitive to whether a lived trial precedes any binding public vote, not a fixed property of the instrument
148:→ a single population's car-trip count and car-kilometres-travelled moved in opposite directions in the same year, which is only possible because the two are different metrics that respond differently to the same policy
149:→ a city that commits to "cut commuter car journeys 20%" without first fixing whether the metric is trip-count, vehicle-kilometres, or peak-period volume risks being unable to determine after 3 years whether it met its own goal, or risks reporting success on one metric while the metric residents actually experience moves the other way
188:→ scoring the four options against seven weighted criteria anchored to C1–C3 and GT-6?/GT-8? yields weighted totals of 106 (pricing alone), 108 (combination), 77 (free transit alone), and 63 (cycle lanes alone)
189:→ the combination's 2-point margin over pricing-alone flips to a tie under a 2-point change to any one of the political-durability, magnitude, equity, or revenue weights, which is far smaller than the 29–45 point gap separating either from the two lowest-scoring single-lever options
190:→ a congestion-pricing-based strategy, whether alone or combined with dedicated reinvestment, is the stronger single-strategy candidate under the evidence gathered, but choosing between pricing-alone and the combination is a genuinely close call that depends on locally-specific weighting
205:→[2nd] future city councils and transit agencies become financially dependent on toll revenue once it is dedicated to capital budgets, raising the political cost of ever repealing the charge, as observed in London and Stockholm's multi-decade persistence
206:→[2nd] motorists and car-dependent businesses become an organized constituency for revenue diversion or repeal if congestion-relief benefits visibly decay over time, as measured directly in London's benefit decay from 30% to 8%
207:→[3rd] the reinvestment cycle raises the coverage fraction available to transit/cycling levers in later years, so the combination's achievable citywide reduction likely exceeds its year-3 figure in years 4 and beyond even if the 20% target is not met by year 3
208:→ a city adopting the combination should treat legal protection of the revenue-reinvestment link (e.g., a locked capital fund, not a discretionary budget line) as a first-order delivery objective, because both its political survival and its long-run magnitude depend on that link holding
216:→ every chain above resolves to a fact about the levers in general, not a fact fixed independent of a specific city's starting conditions — coverage fraction, existing infrastructure lead time, referendum sequencing, tracked metric, and the local weighting of durability against magnitude are all locally variable
217:→ the right choice is therefore not "which of the three options is best" in the abstract, but a function of six facts a city can actually go and measure: (i) what share of citywide commute trips a plausible pricing cordon or a plausible cycle/transit network would actually capture, (ii) how much unused capacity the existing transit network has today, (iii) the city's density, hill profile, and climate, (iv) whether a binding public vote is legally required for pricing and whether a trial can legally precede it, (v) which underlying goal — congestion relief, emissions, equity, health/safety, or revenue — is actually driving the 20% target, and (vi) the city's capital budget and its legal authority to dedicate new revenue to a locked reinvestment fund
218:→ the decision should be made by scoring the same seven trade-off criteria from C5 against these six locally-gathered facts, rather than by selecting one of the three named interventions in the abstract

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** A mid-sized city should not pick one of the three named interventions in the abstract; it should gather the six local facts named in chain C7 — commute-trip coverage a plausible pricing cordon or cycle/transit network would actually capture, spare transit capacity, density/hill/climate profile, the legal referendum requirement and whether a trial can precede it, the true underlying policy driver, and its capital/revenue-dedication authority — and score the same seven weighted criteria used in C5 against those facts (chain C7). Where a binding public vote is legally required for pricing, sequence it as a time-limited trial followed by a vote, not a cold vote (chain C3), and legally lock any pricing revenue into a dedicated transit/cycling reinvestment fund rather than leaving it to discretionary budgeting (chain C6).

**Key insight:** No single lever, implemented in the form most commonly documented in the real-world cases examined, can mathematically reach a 20%-citywide-cut-in-3-years target on its own — the ceiling is set by the product of each lever's geographic coverage and its per-commuter effectiveness, and even the most optimistic single-lever bracket falls well short of 20% (chain C1). This is not visible from a qualitative comparison of the three options; it only emerges from decomposing "how big" into coverage × effectiveness and bracketing each factor against cited evidence.

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** Congestion pricing is the fastest-acting and best-evidenced single lever (chains C1, C2), but its political durability is not fixed — it depends on implementation sequencing (chain C3) and on whether local law can accommodate a trial-before-vote path. A combination of pricing with dedicated reinvestment narrowly outscores pricing alone in the illustrative trade-off matrix, but that margin is a near-tie that flips under a small change to how a specific city weighs political durability, equity, and raw magnitude against each other (chain C5) — no chain — flagged assumption only for which side of that near-tie any specific city will land on. The combination's added durability and growing magnitude in years 4+ depend on legally protecting the revenue-reinvestment link, which is itself an execution risk, not a guarantee (chain C6, LOW confidence). Free-transit-alone and cycle-lanes-alone score clearly lower on achievable 3-year car-trip magnitude in this evidence base (chain C1, chain C5), even though they carry the strongest documented equity and (for cycling) co-benefit profiles — a city whose dominant underlying goal is equity or public health rather than congestion/emissions relief may reasonably choose differently than this magnitude-weighted ranking suggests (chain C5, chain C7).
